A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GAR-Font work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, references, and supplementary Sections A–G are readable and support reliable comparison, including relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original font-generation experiments, quantitative baseline comparisons, tokenizer and training ablations, scaling analyses, and qualitative results in the main text and appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds adaptation-budget and description-source experiments, post-refinement visual analyses, and Korean and higher-resolution generation examples.

M1.justification: The core tokenizer, autoregressive generator, language-style adapter, and NFA/SE procedures remain unchanged. Appendix F.5 adds a higher-resolution adaptation that modifies G-Tok’s CNN encoder to map 128×128 glyphs into 64 tokens using a downsampling factor of 16.

E1.justification: The Chinese GB2312 datasets and UFSC/UFUC tasks are retained. v2 adds a limited qualitative Chinese-to-Korean synthesis experiment in Appendix F.4 and tests additional textual-input conditions using another captioning model and free-form descriptions in D.3.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains LF-Font, VQ-Font, DG-Font, CF-Font, IF-Font, Diff-Font, and Font-Diffuser. The existing VQ-Font(G), joint-training, and vision-only comparisons also remain. SmolVLM supplies alternative descriptions for GAR-Font rather than serving as a competing font-generation method.

E3.justification: Sections 4.2 and C.4 change the main NFA setting from 128 adaptation glyphs to 8. The new budget experiment evaluates 8, 32, and 128 glyphs with and without SE. Additional description tests use 8 glyphs for caption generation, while the retained original collection procedure uses 40. Appendix F.5 also introduces 128×128 generation. These substantially expand the experimental settings; the original datasets, splits, and metrics remain.

E4.justification: New Appendix D.2/Table S3 tests sensitivity to adaptation-glyph count, and D.3/Table S4 tests robustness to caption source and format. F.3/Figure S11 adds visual comparisons isolating NFA and SE effects, while F.4 adds cross-language generalization examples. The existing architecture, noise-robustness, soft-decoding, scaling, and failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the experimental comparisons. The retained content-confidence distributions concern classifier outputs, not uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the 128-glyph refinement rows with new 8-glyph results; for example, Large-UFSC NFA+SE RMSE is 0.2398 under v1’s 128-glyph setting and 0.2503 under v2’s 8-glyph setting. This is not a same-setting deterioration: the original rows remain in v2 Table S3. v2 also adds 32-glyph and description-source scores and new qualitative results. Numerical entries in main Tables 2–6 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, reward definitions, and scaling-law formulation are unchanged. Equation 7 renames the loss from LSFT to LNFA and standardizes equivalent L1 notation. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three contributions and principal claims: global-aware tokenization, efficient multimodal adaptation, and post-refinement improve font generation, with text reducing visual-reference requirements. The added experiments support these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explains generated descriptions as proxies for unavailable human design descriptions, interprets the new budget and caption-robustness findings, and notes that NFA can introduce fine-stroke distortions that SE mitigates. It also softens the stated 64×64 applicability restriction and discusses Korean and higher-resolution generalization. The existing dense-stroke failure explanation remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link and implementation information for the higher-resolution variant, and documents caption models, formats, and reference counts for the new tests. Conversely, Appendix D.1 removes v1’s disclosure that VQ-Font(G) used 150k training iterations versus 500k for VQ-Font, although Table S2 is unchanged. This omission does not establish a changed training budget.

R1.justification: v2 adds the SmolVLM reference for the new description-source experiment. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing font-generation and autoregressive methods remain substantively unchanged. Several other reference edits update publication metadata for the same works.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording and terminology edits, corrects appendix cross-references, adds an affiliation, and moves and expands acknowledgments. New appendix subsections accommodate the additional experiments, while the overall narrative and section organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds two experimental tables and new figures for refinement stages, Korean synthesis, and higher-resolution generation. It replaces the vision-only comparison examples in Figure 5 and Figure S8 and refreshes the five extensive glyph galleries. Figure 6 and several appendix displays are relocated, with corresponding caption and label revisions. These substantially revise the visual evidence presented.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the few-shot evidence by reporting eight-glyph adaptation in the main comparison while preserving the 128-glyph results and exposing the budget tradeoff in Table S3. Caption-robustness tests and new generalization examples provide useful additional validation. These gains are tempered by qualitative-only Korean and higher-resolution evidence, Table S4’s overly broad superiority wording despite worse values on some FID and accuracy metrics, and removal of the VQ-Font training-budget disclosure. Overall, the evidence supports a limited net improvement.
